build: The Force's crack of the 1990 disk, with Ikari+Talent's trainer, its two options left off (archive.org; side A SHA-1 5597c4896f0a6ada501fb13ad94359063a8c1e29, side B 22f881cff073a4797580f95ca6225903a0bfaa99): all seven levels

exclude: Zero page, the stack, page 2 and the start of page 3: the intro clears zero page from $02 and page 2 before it uses them ($080C, $08B6) and keeps its variables in zero page; in $0300-$033F it only writes the KERNAL's interrupt vector at $0314
Pages 3 to 7 after the hand-over code: the intro clears pages 4 to 7 at $08B6 and reads none of this, and nor does the hand-over

The screen: each picture writes its own colours here before it is shown ($0A2D, $0D12, $0D48, $0E38, $1036), and $125B the sprite pointers. The file's bytes here are more of the leftover source text; the logo leaves its side columns alone, but the bitmap there is clear, so they colour no pixels
The bitmap each picture is drawn into: the logo screen clears it before anything is shown ($0F19), so the bytes the file leaves here are never read
The RAM under the I/O area: the intro keeps the I/O chips mapped in all the time ($01=$35), so it never reads the RAM here

comments.text: The hand-over to the game, which runs when the intro returns to the wrapper at $53C0 (its JMP $0340). It turns the BASIC and KERNAL ROMs back on ($01=$37), lets the KERNAL set up the I/O chips again ($FDA3), makes the screen the output device and the keyboard the input ($9A=3, $99=0) and copies the 48 bytes at $ECB9 in the KERNAL ROM into the VIC's registers $D000-$D02F, skipping $D020 and $D021. It calls the KERNAL at $E51B and at $FF5E, its PAL or NTSC test, which sets $02A6, puts the KERNAL's own interrupt routine ($EA31) back in $0314, sets the text colour ($0286), border and background to black, clears the screen ($E544), writes A into the SID's 25 registers ($D400-$D418) and turns interrupts on. It ends by loading the file NINJA* from drive 8 to the address the file gives (secondary address 8, $FFBA, $FFBD, $FFD5) and jumping to $080B, the game's start. The intro clears zero page and pages 2 and 4 to 7, but not page 3, so this code is still there when the intro is over.
The name the hand-over loads, NINJA* (six characters, given to SETNAM at $0399): the asterisk lets the drive take the first file whose name starts NINJA.

The intro's entry, called by the wrapper at $53C0 (JSR $0800). It turns interrupts off, maps RAM with the I/O chips and no ROMs ($00=$2F, $01=$35), clears zero page from $02, and clears fire_allowed ($4C), so fire does nothing on the first showing of the logo. It points the IRQ vector at $106C and the NMI vector at $1345, an RTI, and also puts $1071 in the KERNAL's vector at $0314. It selects VIC bank 1 ($4000-$7FFF) through CIA 2, turns off both CIAs' interrupts, and sets up the VIC: multicolour bitmap mode with the screen blanked ($D011=$2B, $D016=$18), the screen at $4000 and the bitmap at $6000 ($D018=$08), all sprites off and unexpanded, border and background black. Both CIA 1 ports become inputs, the raster interrupt is set for line $2F ($1359) and enabled. It clears the intro's memory ($08B6), starts the tune ($B000), turns interrupts on and falls into the main loop.

The main loop. Each pass calls the eight steps of the sequence in turn, and each step returns at once unless its moment has come: the logo screen ($08D6), the four tile channels ($0C19), the lightning colours ($0CF4), the start of the figure scene ($0D7E), the lamps going out ($0DB9), the next flash of lightning ($0DD7), the vision in the window ($0E0B) and the city picture ($0EEB). It never leaves: the intro ends from inside the logo screen ($0B85).
Clears the intro's working memory: zero page from $02 to $FF, page 2 and pages 4 to 7 ($0400-$07FF), and then sets logo_due ($49) to 1, so the main loop shows the logo first.

The logo screen, run when logo_due ($49) is set. It blanks the screen, clears the bitmap ($0F19), draws the logo ($0985) and shows it, then sets logo_countdown ($3A) to 500 frames, ten seconds on a PAL machine. While the credits scroller runs ($3D bit 7) it only waits. When the countdown reaches 0 it goes on to the temple ($092C). Before that, once fire_allowed ($4C) is set, fire on joystick port 2 ($DC00 bit 4) ends the intro ($0B85); so does the paddle line POTX: the loop selects it with $80 in $DC00, waits 128 loops for the reading to settle, reads $D419 and puts $7F back in $DC00, and a reading below $80 ends the intro as fire does. On the first showing fire_allowed is still 0, so the logo always stays its full ten seconds.

The temple scene, which follows the logo. With the screen blanked it copies the temple picture from $E000 into the bitmap ($0B5A), sets its colours with the lamps alight ($0D12) and resets every channel ($0962). It sets scene_timer ($4A) to 250 frames, starts sprite sequence 0 (the seated figure) and tile scripts 0 and 1 on channels 0 and 1 (the two lamp flames), sets the sprites' shared colours to light blue and black, waits for raster line 128 and shows the picture.

Stops everything that moves: the four tile channels' scripts, steps and delays ($22-$2D), the eight sprites' animations, frame steps and delays ($02-$19), the sprite sequence's step and delay ($44, $43), logo_due ($49), the flash count ($46) and the fade step ($47).

Draws the logo screen: 160 calls of $0996 copy the logo's bitmap a byte column at a time, and 20 calls of $0A2D its colours a cell column at a time. The logo is 20 cells wide and fills all 25 rows, in columns 10 to 29.

Copies byte X (1 to 160) of each of the logo's 25 bitmap rows: from $BC42+X plus 160 for each row, to $604F+X plus 320, which puts the logo in columns 10 to 29 of the bitmap. The 25 load and store pairs are written out, one for each row, with no loop.
Copies cell column X (0 to 19) of the logo's colours for all 25 rows: colour RAM from $8B3D (to $D80A+X, 40 a row) and the screen's colour pairs from $8D31 (to $400A+X), 20 bytes a row in each table.

Copies the temple's bitmap, 32 pages from $E000-$FFFF to $6000-$7FFF. It writes the source and destination into the LDA and STA at $0B72 and $0B75 and steps their high bytes a page at a time. The last 192 bytes it copies ($FF40-$FFFF) land past the 8,000 bytes the VIC shows.
The source and destination of this copy are written at $0B5A-$0B6B and stepped a page at a time.
The low byte of the LDA's address at $0B72, which $0B5C sets to $00.
The high byte of the LDA's address at $0B72: $E0 to start, one more each page.
The low byte of the STA's address at $0B75, which $0B66 sets to $00.
The high byte of the STA's address at $0B75: $60 to start, one more each page.

Ends the intro. It drops the return address of the main loop's JSR $08D6, so its RTS returns to the wrapper at $53C3, which jumps to the hand-over at $0340. Before that it turns interrupts off, blanks the screen, silences the SID ($D418=0), turns the raster interrupt off and acknowledges any that is pending.

An older way into the game that nothing calls. It blanks the screen, turns off the raster interrupt and the sound, turns the KERNAL ROM on ($01=$36) and loads the file named at $0C17, L2, from drive 8 to $A000. With all ROMs and I/O off ($01=$34) it copies $A000-$CFFF to $D000-$FFFF, a page at a time until the destination's high byte wraps to 0. It then pushes $07FF, so that the KERNAL load's RTS goes to $0800, changes the name to L1 ($0BF9 decrements the 2), and jumps into LOAD as logical file 1 with secondary address $FF ($0C00-$0C06); any secondary address other than 0 makes LOAD put L1 at the address its file gives. The wrapper at $53C0 and the hand-over at $0340 replace all of this.
The high byte of the old stub's LDA $A000,X, one more each page.
The high byte of the old stub's STA $D000,X, one more each page; the copy stops when it wraps to 0.
The two-character file name the stub at $0B9F loads, L2, which it changes to L1 for its second load. The byte after it is the first of the code at $0C19.
The 2 of L2, which $0BF9 decrements to make L1.

Steps the four tile channels, called once a pass of the main loop ($089E) and once more by $0D9A, which uses it to draw the unlit lamps at once. A channel runs while its script number has bit 7 set ($22-$25) and moves on when its delay ($2A-$2D, counted down every frame at $10DA) is 0. It then reads its script's header from $17A6: the delay to the next step, the width in bytes and the height in cell rows of each tile, and where in the bitmap it goes. Each step is a tile number, drawn by $0C79. $FC starts the script again, $FD and a number change to another script, and $FE or $FF stop the channel (the script number becomes 2 or 3, without bit 7).

Draws tile A into the bitmap: the tile's address comes from $1804 (low bytes) and $1818 (high), and it copies tile_width ($3F) bytes for each of tile_rows ($40) cell rows to tile_destination ($36), stepping 320 bytes, one cell row, at a time. It keeps X in the operand of the LDX at $0CAF, which gives it back.
The operand is written at $0C84 with the caller's X.
The operand of the LDX at $0CAF, where $0C84 keeps the caller's X.

Replaces cell rows 13 to 17 of the temple picture, the heads and shoulders of the kneeling ninjas in front, with the 1,600 bytes at $84FD: ten copies of 160 bytes, $7040-$767F. $0DD7 calls it at the second flash of lightning.

While channel 2 runs script 6, the lightning in the window ($24=$86), this picks a colour change from nine-entry tables by the channel's step ($28), which is 1 to 8 whenever this runs, so entry 0 is never used ($0C19 draws the first tile and moves the step on before this routine first sees it): the routine from $1361 and $136A, written into the JMP at $0D0E, sets the temple's dark colours ($0D48) or, for steps 3 and 4, the colours with the lamps alight ($0D12), and $1373 gives the sprites' first shared colour, white during those two steps and light blue otherwise.
The target is written at $0CFC-$0D05: $0D12 or $0D48.
The low byte of the JMP at $0D0E, the flash step's colour routine.
The high byte of the JMP at $0D0E.

Sets the temple's colours as it first appears, the lamps alight with an orange glow: 1,000 bytes of colour RAM from $2DF4 and 1,000 bytes of screen colour pairs from $31DC, four pages at a time, the last overlapping the third.
Sets the temple's dark colours, used from the figure scene on, with no glow around the lamps: colour RAM from $35C4 and the screen's colour pairs from $39AC.

Starts the figure scene, once sprite sequence 0 is still holding ($42=$80) and the 250 frames of scene_timer ($4A) are up. It sets the dark colours ($0D48), puts tile scripts 2 and 3 on channels 0 and 1 and runs them at once, which draws both lamps unlit, then starts sprite sequence 1, in which the figure rises, and tile scripts 4 and 5, the smoke above the lamps.

Once sprite sequence 1 has reached step 13, when the figure stands, and channel 0 is still running, this puts tile scripts 2 and 3 on channels 0 and 1 again: both lamps are drawn unlit once more, which ends the smoke. It does this on every pass while channel 0's script has bit 7 set, and each time sets both channels' steps back to 0, so they never reach the $FE that would stop them: the unlit lamps are drawn again every frame or so until $1323 stops the channels.

From step 13 of sprite sequence 1, while fewer than five flashes have come ($46) and scene_timer is out, this starts the next flash: tile script 6 on channel 2, the lightning in the window, with scene_timer set to 50 frames. At the second flash it also redraws the kneeling ninjas ($0CB2). Its test against starting a flash while one runs compares channel 0's script with 6, not channel 2's, so it never succeeds (channel 0 holds script 2, $82, from the lamps going out on); the 50 frames keep the flashes apart, as the lightning takes at least 24 (eight steps of 3 frames; about 27 in a simulation, because while a flash runs each pass of the main loop also copies some 2,000 colour bytes and takes about a frame).

After the fifth flash, unless the city is due ($48) or channel 2 is already on script 6 or 7, this starts the vision: tile script 7 on channel 2, a crackling glow over the window and round the standing figure, drawn from three tiles, sets the sprites' shared colours to light blue and white and scene_timer to 250 frames, then colours the window's cells ($0E38).
Colours the 10 by 14 cells of the window for the vision: screen colour pairs from $8FB1 to columns 15 to 24 of rows 0 to 13 ($400F on), and colour RAM from $8F25 ($D80F on), ten bytes a row.

The last picture. When the fade to white is over ($48 set) and scene_timer is out, it clears the bitmap, draws the city at night with the masked ninja ($0F60, $1036), waits for raster line 128 and shows it for 250 frames. It then clears city_due ($48) and sets logo_due ($49) and fire_allowed ($4C), so the logo comes back and fire now ends the intro.
Clears the bitmap, $6000-$7F3F: 25 passes, one a cell row, of two stores of 160 bytes each, whose addresses it writes into the STAs at $0F32 and $0F35 and moves on 320 bytes a pass.
The two store addresses are written at $0F19-$0F29 and moved on at $0F3B-$0F59.
The low byte of the first STA's address at $0F32, moved on 320 bytes a pass.
The high byte of the first STA's address at $0F32, $5F to start.
The low byte of the second STA's address at $0F35, 160 bytes after the first.
The high byte of the second STA's address at $0F35, $60 to start.
Draws the city picture's bitmap: 160 calls of $0F69.

Copies byte Y (1 to 160) of each of 34 half-rows of the city picture: from $903C+Y to $64FF+Y, both stepping 160 bytes, so the 5,440 bytes at $903D-$A57C fill cell rows 4 to 20 of the bitmap ($6500-$7A3F). The 34 pairs of instructions are written out, with no loop.
Sets the city picture's colours: colour RAM from $A57D and the screen's colour pairs from $A965.

The raster interrupt. It saves A, X, Y and the memory map ($01), maps the I/O chips in ($01=$35) and returns at once if the raster is past line 255. Otherwise it runs this frame's half of the work ($109F), sets the next interrupt's line from $1359 and acknowledges this one. The vector at $0314 points at $1071, after the three saves, because the KERNAL's own interrupt entry saves A, X and Y before it jumps through $0314: so the routine also works with the KERNAL ROM in.

Alternates the two halves of the interrupt's work: raster_phase ($3C) flips between 0 and 1, the old phase picks the raster line to wait for ($135B: $33 or $FB) and the routine, written into the JMP at $10C0 from $135D and $135F: $10C3 at the top of the screen and $10D0 at the bottom.
The target is written at $10AC-$10B5: $10C3 or $10D0.
The low byte of the JMP at $10C0, this frame's half of the work.
The high byte of the JMP at $10C0.
The work done at line $33, once a frame: the tune ($B003), the timers ($10DA), the keys ($1105) and the credits scroller ($112E).
The work done at line $FB, once a frame: the sprite sequence ($11CA), the sprites' animations ($125B) and the fade to white ($1301).
Counts down, by one a frame and stopping at 0: the four tile channels' delays ($2A-$2D), the logo's two-byte countdown ($3A), scene_timer ($4A) and fade_timer ($4B).

Reads the two keys in the table at $1384: it makes CIA 1 port A an output ($DC02=$FF), and for each entry selects the row, masks the column read from $DC01 and stores the result, 0 while the key is held, then makes port A an input again so the joystick can be read. The table holds 1 (row 7, column 0) and L (row 5, column 2); only L is used ($1187).

The hidden credits scroller. While credits_state ($3D) has bit 7 set, every fourth frame it takes the next character of the text through the pointer at $8000: $24, a dollar sign, ends the text (credits_state becomes $24); a space is glyph 0, and any other character its code less $40, so A to Z are glyphs 1 to 26. It copies the glyph's eight bytes from $8425 to $1A-$21, and every frame $1197 scrolls them in. When the scroller is not running, on the logo screen ($49 set), holding L ($1387 = 0) starts it from the beginning of the text.

Scrolls the credits one multicolour pixel to the left: twice over, for each of the eight pixel rows, it shifts the next bit of the incoming glyph ($1A-$21) into the right of a strip of 12 cells of the bitmap and rolls the row along, from $7C48 down to $7BF0, which is columns 14 to 25 of cell row 22 on the logo screen. scroll_phase ($3E) counts the frames, so a glyph, eight bits or four multicolour pixels wide, takes four frames.

Steps the sprite sequence while sprite_sequence ($42) has bit 7 set: when sequence_delay ($43) is 0 it reads the next entry through $138D. An entry below $FC is a formation, set by $121E, which also gives the next delay; $FC starts the sequence again, $FD and a number store that number as the sequence, but the handler goes back to $11CE with A=0, so that step is read from sequence 0's table and the new sequence starts at its second entry on the next step (no sequence uses $FD), $FE stops the sequence and every sprite, and $FF steps back one entry and sets that formation again, which holds the picture.

Sets formation A, from the record whose address is at $13B0 (low bytes) and $13C7 (high): the delay to the next step, then for each of the eight sprites an animation number (bit 7 set to show it) and a position. It starts each animation from its first frame and places each sprite, adding 62 to X and 8 to Y.

Runs the eight sprites' animations. A sprite whose delay ($12-$19) is not yet 0 keeps its frame. Otherwise it is turned off, and if its animation ($02-$09) has bit 7 set, the record from $161D gives the delay, the colour and the frames: a frame below $FC becomes the sprite's pointer, plus $10 because the sprites start at $4400, and the sprite is turned on again. $FC starts the frames again; $FD and a number store that number as the animation, but the handler goes back to $1270 with Y still the offset of that byte in the old record, not twice the number, so that step loads a record pointer from the wrong place in $161D (no animation uses $FD); and $FE stops it.

Sets sprite X's colour from its animation's second byte, or to $83 (cyan, multicolour) once channel 2 runs the vision ($24 is $87 or more); bit 7 of the value makes the sprite multicolour, and bit 6 of the animation's own byte doubles its width.

While the vision is on ($24=$87) and both scene_timer and fade_timer are out, it steps the background through the eight colours at $137C, one every five frames. After the eighth it ends the vision ($1323).

Ends the vision: blanks the screen, sets the background back to black, stops the sprite sequence, the tile channels and every sprite, sets city_due ($48) and gives scene_timer 50 frames before the city appears.
The NMI routine, a lone RTI, so the RESTORE key does nothing during the intro.
A JMP $0800 that nothing reaches.
Each sprite's bit in the VIC's sprite registers, $01 to $80, for sprites 0 to 7.
The same eight bits inverted, $FE to $7F, to turn one sprite's bit off.
The two lines the raster interrupt is set for, $2F (the top half of the work) and $F7 (the bottom).
The lines $109F waits for before it starts each half: $33 and $FB, four lines after the interrupt.
The two halves of the interrupt's work, $10C3 and $10D0, low bytes then high.
The high bytes of the two halves' addresses, $10 and $10.

The colour routine for each value of channel 2's step during a flash of lightning, nine entries, low bytes then high: the dark colours ($0D48) for steps 0 to 2 and 5 to 8, the colours with the lamps alight ($0D12) for steps 3 and 4. The step is 1 to 8 whenever $0CF4 reads it (a flash is eight tiles), so entry 0 is never used.
The high bytes of the nine flash routines' addresses, all $0D.

The sprites' first shared colour for each value of channel 2's step during a flash, nine entries: light blue ($0E), and white ($01) for steps 3 and 4. The step is 1 to 8 whenever $0CF4 reads it, so entry 0 is never used.
The fade to white, one background colour every five frames: black, blue, dark grey, purple, light blue, cyan, light green and white.

The keys $1105 reads, three bytes each: the result (0 while the key is held), the row to select and the column's bit. The first is the 1 key (row 7, column 0, result at $1384), which nothing reads; the second L (row 5, column 2, result at $1387), which starts the credits. A row of $FF at $138B ends the table.
The first key's row: $7F selects row 7. $1105 reads every entry's row as $1385,X.
The first key's column bit, $01 for column 0, read as $1386,X.
The L key's result, 0 while it is held, which starts the credits ($1187), then its row ($DF, row 5) and column bit ($04, column 2).
The two sprite sequences' addresses: $1391 and $1393.
The high bytes of the sequences' addresses, read as $138E,Y.
Sprite sequence 0, the temple: formation 0, the seated figure, then $FF, which sets it again and again until $0D7E starts sequence 1.

Sprite sequence 1, the figure rising: formations 1 to 13, in which it lifts its head and stands, then 16, 15, 14, 15, 16, 13, 17, 18, 19, 18, 17 and 13, which step the head's sprite back and forth through other frames, then 20, 21 and 22, and $FF holds the last.
The 23 formations' addresses, low bytes then high.
The high bytes of the 23 formations' addresses.

The note's second byte ($B795): its top six bits are the note's length in ticks ($B7C8-$B7D2) and its low two bits the instrument number's high two bits ($B81D-$B824). $B539-$B53C are four bytes nothing reads or writes.

Each voice's frequency for its second sound, high byte: the note's pitch plus 12 times the instrument's byte 5, looked up in the note frequencies as the note starts ($B883-$B8A8). MusicWriteSid writes it, with the carry from the detune, while the second sound is on ($B9CC).

Each voice's frequency for its first sound, high byte: the note's pitch plus the instrument's byte 4 plus 12 times its byte 24, looked up as the note starts ($B8B1-$B8DB), then moved by the vibrato ($B68A, $B6BF). Written, with the carry from the detune, while the first sound plays ($B9F3).

Each voice's frequency for its second sound, low byte ($B8AE), which MusicWriteSid writes with the detune added ($B9C0). As the note starts it holds 12 times the instrument's byte 5 for a moment ($B897).

Each voice's frequency for its first sound, low byte ($B8E1), moved by the vibrato ($B683, $B6B5) and written with the detune added ($B9E7). As the note starts it holds the instrument's byte 4 plus 12 times its byte 24 for a moment ($B8C5-$B8D0).

Each voice's pulse width for its second sound, high byte: the instrument's byte 43 as a note starts ($B86B), written while the second sound is on ($B9D2); for voice 2 with the filter on it is the cut-off's high byte ($BA77).
Each voice's pulse width for its first sound, high byte: the instrument's byte 45 as a note starts ($B879), moved by the pulse sweep ($B715, $B747) and written while the first sound plays ($BA0E).

Starts the tune: copies the three voices' start pointers into $F0-$FB, sets each voice's note counter to 1 so its first tick reads a note, sets the volume to 15 and music_on ($FF). The two runs of NOPs are code taken out.

Plays one frame of the tune, unless music_on ($FF) is 0. For each voice in turn: every eighth frame is a tick (the voices' tick counters start at 1, 2 and 3, so they tick on different frames), and when the note's ticks are used up it reads the next note ($B789). Moves the voice's frequency up by the instrument's bytes 29 and 30 while byte 27's count of frames runs down, then down by bytes 31 and 32 while byte 28's count runs down, and over again. Each turn lasts its count of frames, and the frequency moves on all but the last of them, where the direction turns. A note starts going down, for half of byte 28's count; a count of 0 slides on without turning.
Waits out the instrument's pulse delay (byte 33), then sweeps the pulse width ($B6F7) until byte 34's count has run down to 1, or for ever when it is 0.

Moves the pulse width up by bytes 37 and 38 while byte 35's count of frames runs down, then down by bytes 39 and 40 while byte 36's count runs down, and over again. Each turn lasts its count of frames, and the width moves on all but the last of them, where the direction turns; a count of 0 sweeps on without turning. The store that reloads the fall's count ($B75C) has no index, so it always writes voice 0's count: on voices 1 and 2 the second fall has a count of 0 and goes on to the end of the note.

On two frames of every four counts the instrument's byte 3 down, and at 0 swaps the voice between its two sounds (music_second_on) and starts the count again; then moves to the next voice, or to the SID at $B9AB.
Reads the voice's next note, two bytes, from its pattern. $00 $00 ends the pattern, and the next two bytes of the voice's order list give the next pattern.
Reads the next byte of voice X/2's pattern and moves its pointer on.
Reads the next byte of voice X/2's order list and moves its pointer on.

Starts a note. The high byte's top six bits are its length in ticks. Pitch 63 in the low six bits is a rest: the rest waveforms (bytes 23 and 42) of the voice's current instrument are set and nothing else. Otherwise the instrument number is the low byte's top two bits with the high byte's low two above them; the voice's control register gets byte 23 at once, from the instrument the voice played before, since $FD/$FE still points at it ($B7F8); the new instrument's address is $B272 plus 47 times its number, and from it come the two sounds' frequencies (through $B477 and $B4D1: the first from the octave, byte 24, times 12 plus the transpose, byte 4, plus the pitch, the second from byte 5 times 12 plus the pitch), pulse widths and waveforms, the envelope, the vibrato, pulse sweep and swap counts, and the detune, byte 2 times the voice's number.

Writes the three voices to the SID: envelope, frequency (plus the detune), pulse width and waveform, from the second sound's values while music_second_on is set. On voice 2, an instrument with byte 17 bit 0 set turns on the low-pass filter ($BA54); otherwise it sets resonance $F with no voice filtered and volume 15. When voice 2's order list has run out ($FA = $43) it starts the tune again.
